newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Britain wins 400 mln pound BMW plant.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Britain wins 400 mln pound BMW plant.

text.p: German car giant BMW's Rover unit said on Friday it would build a new generation engine in Britain to power top-of-the-range cars in a 400 million pound ($666 million) project.

After what British Trade Minister Ian Lang described as "hard-headed negotiations" with Rover Group Chief Executive Walter Hasselkus, terms were agreed last night for the West Midlands venture, which will be backed by a government grant.

The new state-of-the-art engine plant at Hams Hall will be able to produce around half a million four cylinder petrol engines, from 1.6-2.0 litres capacity, a year for both Rover and its German parent, Rover said.

And with work starting almost immediately on the greenfield site, Rover hopes to start churning out engines in 1999 in a project that will safeguard around 1,500 jobs at Rover and around 5,000 more in the automotive components supply industry.
"I am delighted that we have won this prestigious project against stiff competition. It is magnificent news for Britain," Lang said in a statement.
"I welcome the commitment BMW Group is making to investment in Rover's long term future. This is a mark of confidence in Rover's future potential," he added.
Hasselkus denied that talks had been hampered over the size of the British government grant for the project, insisting that BMW was investing in Britain for mainly long-term strategic reasons.
"We could have gone outside the European Union...we could have secured a much higher grant. But strategic reasons have also played a part," he told a news conference.
Trade unions welcomed the deal, saying that they had lobbied hard to win grant aid to secure the project.
"This is great news for the UK and for the future of maniufacturing in the West Midlands," said the Transport and General Union, Britain's major motor industry union.

Rover's current main volume engine manufacturer is in Longbridge, also in the Midlands. It manufactures about 290,000 engines a year mainly for the highly-successful K-series engines which power Rover's 100, 200 and 400 and 600 and 800 cars.
In the future, the factory and the 6,000 employees that currently manufacture engines may focus more on vehicle assembly, a spokesman said.
Prime Minister John Major welcomed the Rover move as "very good news for Britain".
"What we have seen over recent months is a whole group of international investors beating their way to Britain in order to invest large sums of money," Major said.
About 1,000 U.S. companies are currently investing in Britain, 400 German firms and around 200 Japanese, a spokeswoman for the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) said.
Germany alone had invested 5.80 billion pounds ($9.65 billion) in Britain at the end of 1994, she added.

The biggest inward investment in Britain in terms of both jobs created and capital investment was by LG Group of Korea which invested 1.1 billion pounds creating 6,100 jobs at a semi-conductor plant in south Wales in July.

As well as regional selective assistance grants, Britain offers investors low corporate and personal taxation, an open market, a relatively stable political and economic environment and a reasonable transport and good telecom infrastructures.
One key attraction is a flexible workforce and cheaper manufacturing due to relatively low labour and social costs.

Figures from the Department of Trade and Industry's Invest in Britain Bureau (IBB) show that foreign-owned companies provide 18 percent of manufacturing employment and around 40 percent of all of Britain's manufactured exports.
Since 1979, inward investment has created 600,000 jobs -- mainly in the manufacturing industry.
